Czech Republic.rationale: Czech Republic field a recognizable mid-tier European squad with genuine top-flight quality up front in Patrik Schick (Leverkusen) and Adam Hlozek, plus a reliable midfield anchor in Tomas Soucek and experienced defenders (Coufal, Ladislav Krejci, Hranac). However, the actual tournament evidence is poor: 0W-1D-2L with just 2 goals in 3 games (0.67/game) against Mexico, South Africa and Korea, with low possession (~43%) and modest on-target output. The strong pre-tournament numbers (2.22 goals/game) came largely against minnows like Gibraltar (6-0), San Marino and Guatemala, so they inflate the picture; the competitive draws with Denmark and Ireland are a fairer reflection. Coaching upheaval (Koubek installed late, Dec 2025) adds instability. The attack is capable of generating chances but has been wasteful, hence a slightly below-average off_rating. The defense looked exposed against tournament-level pace, conceding three to Mexico, suggesting a moderately leaky back line. Overall a solid-but-unremarkable side likely to struggle against the field's stronger nations.

Mexico.rationale: Mexico look like an above-average but not elite side. The tournament run is genuinely encouraging: four clean-sheet wins including a controlled 2-0 over a decent Ecuador, and they were competitive in a 2-3 loss to England (20 shots, 82 dangerous attacks) rather than being outclassed. Pre-tournament draws with Portugal and Belgium plus home advantage as co-hosts add real value. However, the squad ceiling is modest: Edson Álvarez anchors a functional midfield, but the attack relies on a 35-year-old Raúl Jiménez and Julián Quiñones, with Santiago Giménez inconsistent at international level — hence roughly 1.6 goals scored across the five WC games with only ~4.2 shots on target per game. Defensively they've been organized under Aguirre (four clean sheets, only conceding to England), though the back line (Montes, Vásquez, Gallardo) can be exposed by top-tier attacks as England showed. Historically Mexico exits in the round of 16; with home support and current form they can beat mid-tier sides but would likely be second-best against true contenders. Off ~1.55 (competent, not devastating), def ~1.15 (well-drilled but vulnerable to elite forwards) — a legitimate dark horse rather than a contender.

South Africa.rationale: South Africa under Hugo Broos are a well-organized, hard-working side built almost entirely from the domestic league (Sundowns/Pirates core) plus Lyle Foster, with Ronwen Williams a genuinely good keeper. Their 2023 AFCON bronze and disciplined structure show up in the data: only 1 goal per game conceded at this World Cup, including a 1-0 win over Korea Republic and a draw with Czech Republic, so the defence is close to tournament-average despite modest individual quality. The attack is the clear limitation — 0.5 goals per game at the finals, just 2.75 shots on target per match, and pre-tournament goals came against weak opposition (Rwanda, Zambia, Nicaragua); they struggled to create against Mexico (3 shots) and Canada. No elite creators or a proven international-level striker (Foster is inconsistent, Makgopa/Rayners are domestic-level). Against an average World Cup side they'd be expected to score slightly under 1 and concede around 1.3. Competitive and awkward to beat, but lacking the firepower and top-end talent to be more than a group-stage battler.

Host advantage helps, but they profile as a mid-pack team: capable of ~1.4 goals against an average World Cup side while conceding around 1.3-1.4. Tournament pedigree is thin (winless in 2022). Solid but not a dark horse — they haven't beaten a strong team in this window.

Embolo, Ndoye and the emerging Manzambi are decent but there's no elite finisher, which historically caps Switzerland at round-of-16/QF exits despite consistent qualification. Pre-tournament wobbles (3-4 vs Germany, draws with Kosovo and Australia) hint the defence isn't impregnable when stretched by top attacks. Net: clearly above the average World Cup team — organized, hard to beat, moderately potent — a legitimate dark horse capable of a deep run via defence and set pieces, but short of true contender firepower.

Paraguay.rationale: Paraguay under Alfaro are a classic low-block, defense-first CONMEBOL side. Tournament data confirms it: 29.6% possession, only 7 shots (1.6 on target) per game, and 0.6 goals/game across five World Cup matches. The attack lacks a reliable finisher — Sanabria and Avalos are aging, Enciso and Almiron provide flashes but no consistent output, and their goals came against Türkiye and Germany in tight games rather than from sustained creation. Defensively they are organized and competitive: Gustavo Gomez, Alonso, and Alderete anchored clean sheets vs Australia and Türkiye and a 1-1 with Germany, with only narrow losses to France. However, the 1-4 collapse against the USA shows fragility when forced to open up, and the veteran backline (avg 33+ for the core CBs) is vulnerable to pace. Net: they can frustrate stronger teams and steal a result, but the near-total absence of attacking threat caps them. Expected to score well under a goal against an average side while conceding slightly under average thanks to structure — a stubborn but ultimately limited team.

Expect roughly 1.2-1.3 goals against an average side. Emerse Fae has tournament-winning pedigree and the team is organized and hard to beat, but they lack the top-end attacking quality to threaten genuine contenders, placing them as a solid, awkward opponent rather than a dark horse.

Rudi Garcia is a competent but not transformative coach, and the squad's age profile is bifurcated (key men 33-37). This is a top-12-to-16 side that beats weaker teams comfortably but lacks the defensive solidity and clinical edge of true contenders — solid rather than dark horse.

Coach Bazeley has organized them adequately but they lack the firepower and back-line solidity to trouble decent teams.

Spain.rationale: Spain arrives with arguably the deepest and most balanced squad in the field: Rodri and Zubimendi anchoring midfield, Pedri and Yamal in prime creative roles, and a young average age (26.4) with elite pedigree (Euro 2024 winners under De la Fuente). The tournament evidence is exceptional on both sides of the ball: 6W-1D-0L with wins over France (2-0), Portugal, Belgium and Uruguay — genuine top-tier opposition, so these results carry real weight. Defensively they have conceded just 1 goal in 7 World Cup games (0.14/game) against a strong schedule, suppressing chances through 64% possession dominance; against an average side that projects to roughly 0.7 conceded. The attack is very good but not quite ruthless: 1.86/game overall, with some finishing inefficiency (0-0 vs Cape Verde on 27 shots, 2-2 vs Türkiye in qualifying, three pre-tournament draws) and reliance on Oyarzabal for goals rather than a prolific striker. That suggests elite chance creation (17+ shots/game) with slightly below-elite conversion, so ~2.2 expected goals vs an average opponent rather than 2.4+. Overall this is a clear contender — the best defensive profile in the tournament combined with a top-three attack.

Cape Verde Islands.rationale: Bottom-up, Cape Verde is a modest squad: veteran attackers (Ryan Mendes 36, Garry Rodrigues 35, Nuno Da Costa 35), players largely from mid-tier European leagues, and an aging keeper (Vozinha, 40). Yet the tournament evidence is striking and against elite opposition: clean sheets vs Spain and Saudi Arabia, a draw with Uruguay, and a 2-1 win over Argentina. That's real signal — an organized, compact defensive block under a long-tenured coach that has repeatedly frustrated top attacks. Against an average WC side I'd expect them to concede around 1.2 — better than their raw talent suggests but I discount the small 4-game sample and some luck (only 3 shots on target allowed per game is unlikely fully sustainable given 37% possession). Offensively they're limited: 1 goal/game vs elite teams flatters slightly given low shot volume and reliance on transition moments; vs an average opponent ~1.0 expected goals is fair. Pre-tournament qualifying wins over Eswatini/Mauritius mean little, though beating Cameroon and Serbia adds credibility. Overall a well-drilled, hard-to-beat side without the attacking depth of a true dark horse — 'solid' captures a team that punches well above its talent level but has a low ceiling.

The March losses to France (1-3) and Croatia (1-2) suggest they concede more against true elite opposition and that their game control frays there. Overall: a compact, hard-to-beat side that can reach the quarters and threaten anyone, but the finishing deficit and aging creative core keep them a notch below the genuine contenders.

That justifies an offensive rating near the top of the field (~2.1 vs an average side). Defensively the picture is more worrying: 1.5 conceded/game, including 2 to Mexico, 1 to DR Congo, and a wild 6-4 vs France; the back line (Guéhi, Konsa, Stones aging, unsettled fullbacks) has not shown Tuchel's usual structure. Much of that concession came against elite attacks (Argentina, France), so against an average World Cup team I'd expect ~1.2 — slightly better than average but not a shutdown defence. Overall: a clear contender carried by an elite attack, with a defence that keeps them from being fully dominant.

Croatia.rationale: Croatia retain elite tournament pedigree (2018 finalists, 2022 third place) and a proven knockout coach in Dalić, but this cycle shows a team in transition. The attack is functional rather than fearsome: 1.5 goals/game in the tournament, but narrow wins over Panama and Ghana, and the striker pool (Kramarić 35, Budimir 34, Musa, Matanović) lacks a reliable elite finisher. Creativity now leans on aging legends (Modrić 40, Perišić 37) and promising but unproven youngsters (Sučić, Baturina). Defensively, the data is worrying: 1.75 conceded/game at the tournament, including 4 vs England and 2 vs Portugal, plus pre-tournament losses to Brazil (1-3) and Belgium (0-2) — they've lost every match against top-tier opposition this year. Gvardiol is world-class but the backline around him (Šutalo, Pongračić, Ćaleta-Car) is merely solid. Rating: attack modestly above average (1.55), defence slightly worse than average (1.4). Their pedigree, midfield control, and knockout-game know-how keep them a dark horse capable of a deep run, but the underlying numbers suggest they are clearly below the true contenders.

Ghana.rationale: Ghana's attack has been anemic: 0.5 goals per game at the tournament with just 5.75 shots and 1 on target per match, and only 36% possession. Key creative outlet Mohammed Kudus is notably absent from the squad, leaving Semenyo as the main threat with limited support from an aging Ayew and inconsistent Iñaki Williams. Goal contributions across the cycle are shockingly thin (leading scorers with 1 goal). Pre-tournament form was poor against mid-tier opposition (1-5 vs Austria, 0-2 Mexico, losses to Germany and South Korea). Defensively they've been more respectable — conceding 0.75/game at the WC including a 0-0 vs England and narrow 1-2 losses to Croatia and Colombia — suggesting Queiroz has organized a compact low block, but they absorb heavy pressure and the underlying friendly numbers (1.38 conceded) suggest that resilience is fragile. An aging Partey anchoring midfield and a squad short on elite depth places them clearly in the weak tier: hard-working, defensively disciplined, but with almost no goal threat against quality opposition.

Panama.rationale: Panama arrive as a classic CONCACAF mid-tier side with an aging squad (avg 30.1, no established European stars beyond Carrasquilla and Murillo) and it showed at the tournament: three straight losses with zero goals scored. The attack is the clear weakness — only 2.33 shots on target per game and no reliable finisher; pre-tournament goals (1.89/game) came mostly against Dominican Republic, South Africa and other weak opposition, while they shipped 6 to Brazil. Defensively they are organized under Christiansen — narrow 0-1 losses to Croatia and Ghana and a respectable 0-2 vs England show they can stay compact and limit damage — so their concession rate against an average side would be only slightly worse than par, around 1.5-1.6. But an offense that couldn't score once in three games and struggled to create against Ghana even with 62% possession projects to roughly 0.7-0.8 goals vs an average World Cup team. Solid structure, minimal cutting edge: a weak-tier side that keeps games close but rarely wins them at this level.
